opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The core idea behind TorchLean is to close the gap between the neural network you actually train and run and the object you reason about when you try to prove something about it.

Today, a lot of verification work happens on an abstraction of the model: you export it, translate it into some other format, maybe idealize the arithmetic as real numbers, and then run a verifier on that. Every one of those steps is a place where the thing you verified quietly stops being the thing you deployed. With TorchLean, the network is defined directly inside Lean, a proof assistant, using a PyTorch-like interface that people already know. That one definition serves as the executable model and as the mathematical object you prove theorems about. There's no separate translation layer to trust.

The second piece is being honest about numerics. Neural networks run in floating point, not on the real line. So we model floating-point semantics explicitly, which lets you state guarantees that hold for the computation the hardware actually performs, rounding included, rather than for an idealized version of it.

On top of that you get the standard verification toolkit, things like interval bound propagation and other bound-based methods for robustness and safety properties. The difference is that these methods are themselves formalized and checked in Lean. When a verifier says "this network is robust in this region," you aren't just trusting a big piece of unverified software. The certificate is machine-checked.

Why do I care so much about this? Our group works a lot on AI for science and on AI that does mathematics. If you want neural networks to be trusted in high-stakes settings, like surrogate models for physical systems or components of theorem-proving pipelines, "it worked on the test set" isn't good enough. You want guarantees, and you want them about the real artifact. TorchLean is a step toward making formal guarantees a natural part of the deep learning workflow instead of a separate, after-the-fact exercise.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says the network is defined directly inside Lean, where it serves as both the executable model and the object of proof.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about TorchLean is that it closes a gap that has existed for as long as we have been training neural networks. We write models in PyTorch, which is wonderful for expressiveness and speed, but PyTorch has no notion of a proof. On the other side, Lean is a proof assistant where every statement is checked down to the axioms, but it was never designed to talk about a convolution or an attention layer. TorchLean's key capability is that it lets the same object live in both worlds. You can take a trained network, with its actual weights, and get a faithful representation of it inside Lean, so that the thing you prove a theorem about is the thing you deployed, not a hand-written abstraction of it.

That matters because the hard part of verification was never the logic, it was the translation. Historically people would re-implement a model in a verification framework, and then you had to trust that re-implementation. Here the compilation from the computational graph to Lean terms is itself mechanically checked, so there is no gap to trust.

Once you have that, you can state properties the way a scientist or an engineer actually wants to state them. For a neural operator solving a PDE, I can ask Lean to certify that the output respects a conservation law, or that the error is bounded on a whole region of the input space rather than on a finite test set. For a controller, I can prove that it stays within a safety envelope. And when the proof does not go through, that is information too, because Lean points at the exact layer and the exact bound that fails, which is far more useful than a red-team example.

I also want to emphasize the compositional piece. Proofs about individual layers compose, so you do not re-verify the whole network every time you fine-tune. That is what makes it practical at scale rather than a demo on a tiny MLP. To me that is the real capability: verification becomes part of the training loop instead of an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response says a trained PyTorch network can be translated into a faithful representation inside Lean. It does not say networks are defined directly in Lean.

astra-6.text: The key capability is bringing neural-network computations into a formal proof system, so you can reason rigorously about whether a network satisfies a specified property. Testing tells you what happens on the examples you try; formal verification aims to establish that a property holds for every input covered by your assumptions. The important qualification is that the guarantee is only as strong as the specification and how faithfully the formal model represents the actual network.

r001.rationale: The response describes bringing neural-network computations into a formal proof system, but does not say that TorchLean defines the networks directly in Lean.

sol-6.1.text: The key capability is moving from empirical testing to proving that a neural network satisfies a precisely stated property. Testing tells you what happens on the examples you try; formal verification can give you a guarantee across all inputs covered by your assumptions. But the scope matters: you’re proving a specific property under specific assumptions, not that the network is universally correct or safe.

r001.rationale: The response describes proving properties of neural networks, but does not say that TorchLean formalizes them by defining the networks directly in Lean.
